prompt: Which of these runs in the account AWS manages, and not in yours?
hint: The control plane.

choices.text: kube-proxy, on each node
choices.why: It is an add-on, and it runs on your nodes beside your pods.

choices.text: etcd, where the cluster's state is kept
choices.why: Right. etcd and the API server are the control plane AWS runs across three zones.

choices.text: The node group's instances
choices.why: They are EC2 instances in your account, billed at EC2 prices.

choices.text: CoreDNS
choices.why: A Deployment of two pods on your nodes.

prompt: A team gives each of its 10 developers an EKS cluster of their own, in standard support, at 0.10 USD an hour each. What do the control planes cost for a month of 730 hours, in USD?
hint: Clusters times price times hours.

prompt: How does kubectl prove who it is to an EKS cluster with the kubeconfig that aws eks update-kubeconfig writes?
hint: Read the users: part of the file.

choices.text: With a password the command wrote into the file
choices.why: There is no password in it; the user is a command.

choices.text: With a client certificate kept in the file's users section
choices.why: The certificate in the file is the cluster's, used to check the server.

choices.text: It runs aws eks get-token for a pre-signed STS request
choices.why: Right. The API server sends it to STS, which says who signed it, so the Kubernetes user is an IAM principal.

choices.text: The cluster's OIDC issuer signs each request kubectl sends
choices.why: The issuer is for pods taking IAM roles, lesson 13; it signs nothing for kubectl.

prompt: AWS requires an EKS cluster to be given subnets in at least ___ different Availability Zones.
hint: A number.

prompt: A script creates a cluster and then a node group straight away. Against moto it works. What does it need before the second call on AWS?
hint: moto said ACTIVE at once; AWS does not.

choices.text: aws eks wait cluster-active
choices.why: Right. On AWS the cluster is CREATING for several minutes first.

choices.text: A kubectl get nodes that returns at least one node
choices.why: There are no nodes until the node group exists, so this would wait for ever.

choices.text: aws eks update-kubeconfig, which starts the control plane
choices.why: It writes a file on your machine and starts nothing.

choices.text: A sleep of ten seconds after create-cluster
choices.why: Ten seconds is far short of the minutes it takes; a guess is not a wait.

prompt: Which of these are true of the cluster moto created in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: moto keeps records.

choices.text: Its endpoint is a name nothing answers on
choices.why: moto made the name up and runs no API server.

choices.text: It was ACTIVE as soon as it was created
choices.why: On AWS it would be CREATING for several minutes.

choices.text: There is no Kubernetes behind it
choices.why: moto keeps a record of the cluster and nothing else.

choices.text: kubectl get nodes would list the node group's three instances
choices.why: There is no API server, and moto launched no instance.

choices.text: Its OIDC issuer is a real identity provider other services trust
choices.why: It is a URL moto printed; nothing serves it.

prompt: On a brand new EKS cluster, the first pod anybody creates stays Pending. Why?
hint: What does a new cluster come with?

choices.text: The control plane takes an hour to accept pods
choices.why: The control plane is ready when the cluster is ACTIVE.

choices.text: There are no nodes yet
choices.why: Right. Nodes are a separate decision: a node group, Fargate or Karpenter.

choices.text: vpc-cni has not been bought as a separate subscription
choices.why: Add-ons carry no subscription; EKS installs the networking ones at creation.

choices.text: The pod's image is not in ECR
choices.why: A missing image gives ImagePullBackOff on a node, which first needs a node.

prompt: moto answered create-nodegroup with version 1.19 for a cluster of version 1.35. What version does AWS give a new managed node group?
hint: AWS's API reference states it.

choices.text: The oldest version still in standard support
choices.why: Nothing picks the oldest; that would start the group on the clock's last months.

choices.text: 1.19, as moto said
choices.why: That is moto's fixed value, the same for every cluster.

choices.text: Whatever version the AMI type was first released with
choices.why: The AMI type picks an operating system and a processor, not the Kubernetes version.

choices.text: The control plane's, with the newest image
choices.why: Right. A managed node group starts level with the cluster it joins.

prompt: Match each option of create-nodegroup to what it decides.
hint: Lesson 4 and lesson 6 met most of these.

pairs.right: The smallest, largest and current number of nodes
How many nodes a version update takes out at once
The operating system and the processor family
A label on every node that pods are scheduled by
Whether the nodes are bought at the spot discount

right_distractors: The Kubernetes version of the control plane

prompt: A node group needs to grow from 3 nodes to 4. Why is the change made with aws eks update-nodegroup-config and not with aws autoscaling on the group it names?
hint: Whose group is it?

choices.text: aws autoscaling refuses every group whose name starts with eks-
choices.why: No such refusal exists; the point is who manages the group.

choices.text: The group is EKS's to manage, sizes included
choices.why: Right. Changing it behind EKS's back leaves the node group's record wrong.

choices.text: Auto Scaling groups have no desired size
choices.why: Lesson 4 set one on every group.

choices.text: It is cheaper through EKS
choices.why: The instances cost the same whichever API asked for them.

prompt: A Terraform module creates node groups, and its tests run against moto. One test creates a group with minSize 5 and maxSize 2, and it passes. What does the passing test show?
hint: What did moto do with the same values in this lesson?

choices.text: That AWS accepts a minimum above the maximum
choices.why: AWS refuses it; moto checks much less.

choices.text: That EKS swaps the two values around whenever they arrive reversed
choices.why: Nothing swaps them; moto stored them as given.

choices.text: Nothing about the values: moto accepted a group AWS would refuse
choices.why: Right. A configuration moto accepts has not been validated by anybody.

choices.text: That the group will run 9 nodes
choices.why: It will run none, on moto or on AWS.

prompt: Match each add-on to the job it does in the cluster.
hint: Three networking add-ons, and one for storage.

pairs.right: Gives each pod an address from the VPC
Writes the rules that bring a Service's traffic to its pods
Answers DNS for names inside the cluster
Turns a volume claim into an EBS volume

prompt: A t3.medium has 3 network interfaces and 6 IPv4 addresses per interface. With the default vpc-cni, how many pods fit on it?
hint: interfaces × (addresses − 1) + 2

prompt: An instance type has 8 network interfaces and 30 IPv4 addresses per interface. With the default vpc-cni and no prefix delegation, how many pods fit on one node?
hint: The same formula as the lesson, on numbers it did not show.

prompt: aws eks create-addon --addon-name vpc-cni --resolve-conflicts OVERWRITE takes over a copy that somebody had configured by hand. What happens to their settings?
hint: The option is named for what it does.

choices.text: They are kept, and EKS manages the add-on from then on
choices.why: That is closer to PRESERVE, which keeps them.

choices.text: The call fails and nothing changes
choices.why: That is NONE when the values differ.

choices.text: Where they differ from EKS's defaults, EKS's values replace them
choices.why: Right, and a hand-made change is gone without a warning.

choices.text: They are copied into a second, disabled add-on
choices.why: EKS keeps one add-on of each name and no copies.

prompt: A cluster of t3.medium nodes runs small pods that ask for 50 millicores each. New pods stay Pending although every node shows 20% processor use. What is the most likely limit?
hint: What else does every pod need from its node?

choices.text: Each node is out of VPC addresses at 17 pods
choices.why: Right. vpc-cni gives every pod a real address, and a t3.medium has 17 to give.

choices.text: The control plane caps every cluster at a fixed number of pods per zone
choices.why: No such cap was described; the limit here comes from the nodes.

choices.text: kube-proxy has run out of rules
choices.why: kube-proxy writes rules for Services and has no per-node pod limit of this kind.

choices.text: The processor is fuller than the 20% shows
choices.why: The pods asked for little, and 20% is what they use.

prompt: With prefix ___, vpc-cni puts a block of 16 addresses in each slot of an interface, and a node holds many more pods.
hint: The name of the feature, second word.

prompt: Put the steps of moving a cluster from 1.35 to 1.36 in the order AWS documents.
hint: It starts with reading and ends with the nodes.
items: Read the upgrade insights for APIs the next version removes
Upgrade the add-ons to versions published for 1.36
trap: The nodes go last: a kubelet may be older than the API server, never newer.

prompt: Two clusters stay in extended support for 9 months. Extended support adds 0.50 USD an hour to each, over months of 730 hours. How much more do they cost in all than if they had been upgraded, in USD?
hint: Clusters × 0.50 × 730 × months.

prompt: Nobody touched a cluster created with the default upgrade policy, and its version reaches the end of standard support. What happens?
hint: AWS's API reference names the default.

choices.text: AWS upgrades the control plane that day
choices.why: That is what STANDARD does; the default is EXTENDED.

choices.text: It enters extended support at 0.60 USD an hour
choices.why: Right: six times the 0.10 of standard support, and nothing on the cluster announces it.

choices.text: The cluster stops accepting new pods until it is upgraded
choices.why: It keeps working; what changes is the bill.

choices.text: The node groups are upgraded and the control plane stays
choices.why: Nothing upgrades the nodes for you; their upgrade is a call you make.

prompt: A cluster on 1.33, whose nodes are in managed groups, has to reach 1.36. How many times is update-cluster-version called, and what has to happen between the calls?
hint: One minor version per upgrade, and a rule about node groups.

choices.text: Once, straight to 1.36, and the node groups afterwards
choices.why: The control plane moves one minor version per upgrade.

choices.text: Three times, with nothing in between
choices.why: AWS refuses the next upgrade while a managed node group lags behind.

choices.text: Twice, since 1.34 and 1.35 are skipped together
choices.why: Nothing skips versions; 1.33 to 1.36 is three steps.

choices.text: Three times, with every node group brought level after each
choices.why: Right. A managed node group has to match the cluster before the cluster moves again.

prompt: A node group update starts. Which of these will block it, or break something while it runs? Choose all that apply.
hint: Every pod moves at least once.

choices.text: A PodDisruptionBudget asking for 3 of 3 replicas
choices.why: It is never met, so draining stops and the update fails unless forced.

choices.text: A single replica that keeps its state on the node's disk
choices.why: It is evicted, restarted elsewhere, and its state stays on the old disk.

choices.text: A service with no readiness check
choices.why: Its new pods receive traffic before they are ready.

choices.text: maxUnavailable set to 1
choices.why: It makes the update slower and blocks nothing.

choices.text: Nodes labelled role=general
choices.why: Labels decide where pods go and play no part in draining.

prompt: A cluster in standard support (0.10 USD an hour) runs one managed node group of 3 m7g.large on demand, at 0.1301 USD an hour each in sa-east-1. What does a month of 730 hours cost, in USD, to the cent?
hint: Control plane plus nodes; the node group itself adds nothing.

prompt: A pipeline creates a fresh EKS cluster for every pull request and deletes it after the tests. There are 20 a day, and each cluster lives 2 hours at 0.10 USD an hour. What do the control planes cost per day, in USD?
hint: Cluster-hours times the price.

prompt: A team wants 40 small pods on each m7g.large node, which the default vpc-cni stops at 29. Which change raises that limit on the same instance type?
hint: The limit is about addresses on the interfaces.

choices.text: A larger subnet for the node group
choices.why: More addresses in the subnet do not add slots to a node's interfaces.

choices.text: Prefix delegation in vpc-cni
choices.why: Right: a block of 16 addresses per slot instead of one.

choices.text: maxUnavailable raised in the update config of the node group
choices.why: That governs updates and has no effect on how many pods fit.

choices.text: The upgrade policy set to STANDARD
choices.why: It decides what happens when support ends, not how pods are addressed.
